name: Majorelle Blue
lede: Majorelle Blue is a vivid blue-violet named for the French painter Jacques Majorelle, who painted the walls and pergolas of his Marrakech garden in this color during the 1920s and 1930s.

sections.title: A painter's garden wall
sections.body:
Jacques Majorelle, a French Orientalist painter working in Marrakech, built a villa and garden there from 1923 and used an intense cobalt-leaning blue on its walls, fountains and pergolas, a color later named for him [1]. The garden fell into disrepair after his death in 1962 and was restored from 1980 by the fashion designer Yves Saint Laurent and his partner Pierre Bergé, who kept the blue and reopened the grounds as the Jardin Majorelle [1]. Our library lists the hex #6050DC under the person tier, with a strong purplish-blue ISCC-NBS classification 8.2 units from its nearest block [2]. The nearest named colors on file are [[majorelle-blue]], [[iris]] and [[blurple]], at 3.9, 
The swatch on screen reads closer to violet than the wall color most visitors remember, which tends toward a deeper, more saturated cobalt; screen blues compress easily next to a bright white Moroccan sky [2]. Nearby on the wheel sit [[cobalt-blue]] and [[dark-blue|French ultramarine]], the pigments that give that same intensity in paint, and [[french-blue]] sits a little further toward true blue [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: No painting in our 23,781-painting archive carries a close match to Majorelle Blue, covering at least one percent of its canvas, as photographed [3]. That says more about the archive, which leans toward European painting before the twentieth century, than about the color itself [3]. In printed English the two-word phrase does not rise until the 2000s, peaking in the 2010s, well after Majorelle's death, which fits a color named retroactively for a garden that only became famous once it reopened to the public [4].
